title: Soreng on a budget: real costs for 2026
meta_description: What a Soreng trip really costs in 2026: shared jeep fares, homestay rates, Barsey fees and sample 3-night budgets for Rinchenpong, Kaluk and Okhrey.
summary: Soreng is one of the cheapest parts of Sikkim to travel in. Two people sharing can do three nights in Rinchenpong or Okhrey for about ₹6,000–9,000 each using shared jeeps and homestays with meals. A private car is the biggest single cost; homestay food is the best value. All figures are indicative for 2026.

sections.heading: What a budget Soreng trip really costs
paras: Soreng district sits in Sikkim's south-west corner, about 100 km from Siliguri, and almost everything a visitor does here is cheap: walking ridge roads at Rinchenpong and Kaluk, climbing to the old monastery, hiking from Hilley into the Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary, sitting with tea while Kangchenjunga turns pink at sunrise. There are no ropeways, no entry-ticket attractions and no casinos. Your money goes on three things: getting here, a bed, and food.

On a true budget, using shared jeeps and family homestays that include meals, two people sharing a room spend roughly ₹1,800–2,800 each per day once they arrive, plus the journey in and out. Add a reserved small car for the whole trip and the daily figure rises to about ₹3,500–5,000 each. These are indicative 2026 numbers from our own bookings and local rates. Fares and tariffs move every season, so check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Getting there by shared jeep
paras: The cheapest way in is the shared jeep (a Bolero, Sumo or Max with ten seats) from Siliguri. Jeeps for Jorethang leave from the Sikkim Nationalised Transport stand area near Siliguri's main bus terminus through the morning; a handful run direct to Soreng, Kaluk or Rinchenpong, usually before noon. From NJP station or Bagdogra airport you first need an auto or shared cab to Siliguri.

The road runs along the Teesta on NH10 to Melli, where you enter Sikkim, then up the Rangeet valley to Jorethang, the bazaar town at the district's front door. In the monsoon NH10 closes after slides; drivers then come round through Darjeeling and down to Jorethang, which adds one to two hours. From Jorethang, local jeeps climb to Soreng, Rinchenpong, Kaluk, Daramdin and Sombaria. Okhrey and Hilley have very few shared vehicles, so most people reserve a car from Sombaria or Jorethang for the last stretch.
Shared jeeps fill up and then leave. Arrive early, buy the ticket at the counter rather than from a tout, and pay a little extra for the two front seats if you get carsick on hill roads.

sections.heading: Where the cheap beds are
paras: Soreng's best value is the family homestay. In Rinchenpong, Kaluk, Okhrey, Hilley and the villages around Soreng bazaar, most homestays quote a per-person rate that includes dinner, breakfast and often lunch: about ₹1,200–2,200 each in 2026, a little more in the April rhododendron rush and around the October–November holidays. You get a clean double room, usually an attached bathroom with a geyser, and food cooked in the family kitchen.

Small hotels in Soreng bazaar, Rinchenpong and Kaluk charge about ₹1,500–3,000 for a double room without meals. The Soreng district administration lists hotels such as The Orchid Hotel and Hotel Nangjang in Soreng and Hotel Mount View in Rinchenpong. Zostel Rinchenpong has dorm beds for solo travellers. Village resorts in Kaluk and Rinchenpong, with bigger rooms and gardens, start around ₹3,000 a room and are covered in our Rinchenpong and Kaluk stay guide.

At Okhrey, a Sherpa village about 10 km below Hilley, homestays and small lodges such as Sherpa Lodge and Kyilkhor Inn are the base for the Barsey walk. Rooms here are simple and the nights are cold from November to March; ask whether a blanket heater or hot-water bottle is available.

sections.heading: Food and daily spending
paras: If your homestay includes meals you will spend very little on food. Expect rice, dal, a vegetable, a seasonal green such as squash shoots or nettle, pickles, and chicken or pork once or twice; ask if you need it vegetarian. In bazaars at Jorethang, Soreng and Rinchenpong, a plate of momos costs about ₹80–150, a bowl of thukpa ₹100–150 and a rice thali ₹150–250. Tea in a roadside shop is ₹20–30.

Other daily costs are small. The Barsey sanctuary charges a forest entry fee at the Hilley check post, roughly ₹50–100 a person a day with extra for cameras, and Sikkim collects a ₹50 per tourist entry fee at check-in, valid 30 days. Monasteries do not charge, but a donation of ₹50–100 in the box is good manners. A local guide for the Barsey walk is optional and costs about ₹1,000–1,500 for the day.
list: Tea and a snack on the road: ≈ ₹60–120
Bazaar lunch of momos or thukpa: ≈ ₹100–200
Bottle of water: ≈ ₹20–30 (carry a refillable bottle instead)
Barsey entry at Hilley: ≈ ₹50–100 plus camera fee, check current status

sections.heading: Three sample budgets for three nights
paras: These are per person, two people sharing, for three nights from NJP and back, in 2026. They assume one night's food on the road is paid separately. The budget column uses shared jeeps both ways and homestays with meals; the middle column adds a reserved small car for the whole trip; the comfortable column uses a private SUV and a village resort.

sections.heading: Ways to save, and where not to
paras: The biggest saving is to travel as four instead of two. A reserved car costs the same whether it carries two or four people, so a family or two couples cut the transport line in half. The second is to pick one base. Rinchenpong and Kaluk are 3 km apart on the same ridge, and you can walk between them; Okhrey and Hilley are 10 km apart. Two nights in one place costs less than two places with a transfer day in between.

Travel outside the peak weeks if you can. The second half of April, the Durga Puja and Diwali holidays and the Christmas week bring the highest rates in Soreng, while late February, early March, October before the holidays and November after them are quieter and cheaper, with good mountain views.

Do not save on the driver. A cheap car hired from a stranger at Jorethang may not have a valid Sikkim tourist registration, and unlicensed drivers are not allowed to carry tourists to some points. Book through a registered agency or your homestay. And do not skimp on warm layers in winter or on rain gear from June to September: buying them in a village costs more than bringing them.

sections.heading: Cash, cards and phone signal
paras: UPI payments work in most bazaars and many homestays where there is mobile data, but signal is patchy on the Okhrey to Hilley road and inside the sanctuary. Carry enough cash for two or three days. ATMs are found in Jorethang and in larger bazaars such as Soreng, but they sometimes run dry over long weekends, so do not count on one in Okhrey, Hilley or Kaluk. Homestays usually ask for an advance by bank transfer or UPI and the balance in cash at checkout.

Tipping is not expected in homestays, but a few hundred rupees for the family, or for a driver who has waited through a long Barsey walk, is appreciated. If you book a package through us, the price we quote covers the stays, the car and driver, the sanctuary and Sikkim entry fees and our planning; lunches, camera fees, tips and anything personal are extra. We show that split line by line on every journey, so you can compare it with doing it yourself.

faqs.q: How much does a 3-night Soreng trip cost per person?
faqs.a: On shared jeeps and homestays with meals, about ₹6,000–9,000 each for two people sharing, from NJP and back. With a reserved small car for the whole trip it is closer to ₹12,000–14,000 each, and with a private SUV and a village resort about ₹20,000–25,000. All figures are indicative for 2026; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there a shared jeep from Siliguri to Rinchenpong?
faqs.a: A few shared jeeps run direct from Siliguri to Kaluk and Rinchenpong, usually leaving in the morning from the area near the SNT bus stand. If you miss them, take a jeep to Jorethang (3–3.5 h) and change to a local jeep for Rinchenpong (about 2 h). Expect roughly ₹400–600 a seat in total. Timings change, so ask at the counter the day before.

faqs.q: How much is a homestay in Okhrey or Rinchenpong?
faqs.a: Most family homestays in Okhrey, Rinchenpong and Kaluk charge about ₹1,200–2,200 per person a night including dinner and breakfast, sometimes lunch too. Rates rise in April, when the rhododendrons bloom, and during the October and December holidays. Indicative for 2026. Book ahead for April weekends, when Okhrey fills with walkers heading to Barsey.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Barsey Rhododendron Sanctuary?
faqs.a: The forest department collects an entry fee at the Hilley check post. Recent reports put it at about ₹50 a day for Indians and ₹100 for foreigners, with separate charges for still and video cameras. Fees are revised from time to time, so treat these as indicative and check current status before you travel. Keep the receipt until you leave the sanctuary.

faqs.q: Can I visit Soreng without a private car?
faqs.a: Yes for Rinchenpong, Kaluk and Soreng bazaar, which have regular shared jeeps from Jorethang. It is harder for Okhrey and Hilley, where shared vehicles are rare; most people reserve a car from Sombaria or Jorethang for the last 20–30 km. Once you are in Rinchenpong or Kaluk, you can walk to the monastery, viewpoints and the neighbouring village.

faqs.q: Are there ATMs in Rinchenpong, Kaluk or Okhrey?
faqs.a: Do not count on it. ATMs are reliable in Jorethang and in bigger bazaars such as Soreng, but small villages often have none, and machines can run out of cash on long weekends. Carry cash for two or three days. UPI works in many shops and homestays wherever there is mobile data, but signal is weak around Okhrey, Hilley and inside the sanctuary.

faqs.q: When is Soreng cheapest to visit?
faqs.a: Late February to mid-March, the first half of October and late November to mid-December usually have lower homestay rates and fewer visitors, and the mountain views are good in all three windows. The monsoon (June to September) is cheapest of all but brings rain, leeches and occasional road closures. The second half of April is the most expensive and busiest time.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Soreng district?
faqs.a: Indian travellers do not need a special permit for Rinchenpong, Kaluk, Okhrey, Hilley or Soreng, only the ₹50 Sikkim tourist entry fee collected by your hotel and the forest entry fee for Barsey. Foreign nationals need Sikkim's Restricted Area Permit, applied for online on the e-FRRO portal after arrival in India. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.

No. Most homestays include meals in the room rate, and bazaar food is cheap: momos about ₹80–150 a plate, thukpa ₹100–150 and a rice thali ₹150–250. Packaged snacks cost the same as in the plains. Choice is limited in small villages, so tell your homestay in advance if you need vegetarian, Jain or child-friendly food.
